questions.title: Equal time intervals in free fall
questions.subtopic: Equal time intervals in free fall
questions.stem: A package is released from a descending platform with initial downward speed $4.0\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. Air resistance is negligible; use $g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$. What is the ratio of the distance travelled during the third second to that during the first second?
questions.changeNotes: New numerical data and a changed inference or linked modelling task; original wording and recomputed distractors.

verification.method: Author calculation, dimensional and limiting-case checks

steps.text: The distance in the first second is $4(1)+\tfrac12(10)(1)^2=9\,\mathrm{m}$. During $t=2$ to $3\,\mathrm{s}$ it is $[4(3)+5(3)^2]-[4(2)+5(2)^2]=29\,\mathrm{m}$. Equal velocity increments do not imply equal distances. Therefore choose C.

questions.title: Unequal masses in an inelastic collision
questions.subtopic: Unequal masses in an inelastic collision
questions.stem: Carts of masses $m$ and $3m$ approach one another on a frictionless line with equal speeds $v$. They stick together. What fraction of the original total kinetic energy remains as kinetic energy?

sourceAnchors.focus: Momentum and energy in sticking collisions

questions.changeNotes: New numerical data and a changed inference or linked modelling task; original wording and recomputed distractors.

verification.method: Author calculation, dimensional and limiting-case checks
verification.notes: See the named reproducible author checks and worked solution for this question.

steps.text: Taking the lighter cart's motion positive, initial momentum is $mv-3mv=-2mv$. The combined velocity is $-v/2$. Initial energy is $\tfrac12mv^2+\tfrac12(3m)v^2=2mv^2$, and final is $\tfrac12(4m)(v/2)^2=\tfrac12mv^2$. The fraction is $1/4$. Therefore choose A.

steps.text: Useful power is $\dot m(gh+v^2/2)=12(50+2)=624\,\mathrm{W}$. Electrical input is $624/0.60=1040\,\mathrm{W}$. Both potential and kinetic energy gains count as useful output. Therefore choose D.

steps.text: For each rod, thermal resistance is $L/(kA)$. If the thin rod has resistance $R$, the thick rod has $R/4$. Initial series resistance is $5R/4$, while final resistance is $R/2$. At fixed total temperature difference, the rate increases by $(5R/4)/(R/2)=2.5$. Therefore choose C.

questions.title: Gas pressure and molecular speed
questions.stem: A sealed sample of ideal gas expands to twice its original volume. Its pressure rises to $1.5$ times its original pressure. What is the ratio of final to initial rms molecular speed?

sourceAnchors.focus: Kinetic theory and the ideal-gas equation

questions.changeNotes: New numerical data and a changed inference or linked modelling task; original wording and recomputed distractors.
questions.cognitiveDemand: Link physical models, interpret conditions and justify the result.

verification.method: Author calculation, dimensional and limiting-case checks
verification.notes: See the named reproducible author checks and worked solution for this question.

steps.text: For fixed particle number, $T\propto PV$, so $T_2/T_1=(1.5)(2)=3$. Since $v_{\rm rms}\propto\sqrt T$, the speed ratio is $\sqrt3$. The gas expansion alone does not imply cooling when energy is supplied. Therefore choose B.

questions.title: Melting followed by warming
questions.stem: An insulated mixture contains $20\,\mathrm g$ of ice and $80\,\mathrm g$ of water, both at $0^\circ\mathrm C$. It receives $8.00\,\mathrm{kJ}$. Use latent heat of fusion $3.30\times10^5\,\mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}}$ and water specific heat capacity $4200\,\mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$. What is the final temperature?

sourceAnchors.focus: Latent heat and changes of internal energy

questions.changeNotes: New numerical data and a changed inference or linked modelling task; original wording and recomputed distractors.
questions.cognitiveDemand: Link physical models, interpret conditions and justify the result.

verification.method: Author calculation, dimensional and limiting-case checks
verification.notes: See the named reproducible author checks and worked solution for this question.

steps.text: Melting the ice requires $0.020(3.30\times10^5)=6600\,\mathrm J$. The remaining $1400\,\mathrm J$ warms all $0.100\,\mathrm{kg}$ of water. Hence $\Delta T=1400/(0.100\times4200)=3.33\,\mathrm K$. The mass to warm includes the melted ice. Therefore choose D.

questions.title: Opening a parallel branch
questions.stem: A cell of emf $18\,\mathrm V$ and internal resistance $2.0\,\Omega$ supplies a $4.0\,\Omega$ resistor in parallel with a $12\,\Omega$ resistor. The $12\,\Omega$ branch is opened. What happens to the terminal potential difference and the current in the $4.0\,\Omega$ resistor?
questions.changeNotes: New numerical data and a changed inference or linked modelling task; original wording and recomputed distractors.
questions.cognitiveDemand: Link physical models, interpret conditions and justify the result.

verification.method: Author calculation, dimensional and limiting-case checks
verification.notes: See the named reproducible author checks and worked solution for this question.

options.label: A
options.text: Terminal potential difference decreases; the $4.0\,\Omega$ current increases.

options.label: D
options.text: Terminal potential difference increases; the $4.0\,\Omega$ current decreases.

steps.text: Initially external resistance is $3.0\,\Omega$, cell current $3.6\,\mathrm A$, terminal voltage $10.8\,\mathrm V$ and $4\,\Omega$ current $2.7\,\mathrm A$. After opening, cell current is $18/6=3.0\,\mathrm A$, terminal voltage $12\,\mathrm V$ and branch current $3.0\,\mathrm A$. Reduced internal voltage loss raises both requested quantities. Therefore choose C.

questions.title: Refraction of sound
questions.stem: Sound travels from air into water at an incidence angle of $10^\circ$ to the normal. The speeds are $340\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ and $1480\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. What is the approximate refraction angle, and what happens to frequency?

steps.text: For waves $\sin\theta_1/\sin\theta_2=v_1/v_2$, giving $\sin\theta_2=(1480/340)\sin10^\circ=0.756$. Thus $\theta_2\approx49^\circ$. Boundary oscillations preserve frequency; the wavelength increases. Therefore choose B.

questions.title: Changing the second optical medium

steps.text: With air index $1$, $n_s=1/\sin30^\circ=2.00$. At the new boundary, $\sin c=n_l/n_s=1.33/2=0.665$, so $c=41.7^\circ$. The solid's refractive index has not changed; the index ratio has. Therefore choose A.

questions.title: Comparing spectral redshifts
questions.stem: A spectral line of rest wavelength $500.00\,\mathrm{nm}$ is observed at $500.75\,\mathrm{nm}$ in star X. A line of rest wavelength $650.00\,\mathrm{nm}$ is observed at $650.65\,\mathrm{nm}$ in star Y. Both speeds are much less than $c$. What is $v_X/v_Y$?
questions.changeNotes: New numerical data and a changed inference or linked modelling task; original wording and recomputed distractors.
questions.cognitiveDemand: Link physical models, interpret conditions and justify the result.

verification.method: Author calculation, dimensional and limiting-case checks
verification.notes: See the named reproducible author checks and worked solution for this question.

steps.text: For low speeds, $v/c=\Delta\lambda/\lambda_0$. The ratio is $(0.75/500)/(0.65/650)=1.50$. Comparing shifts alone omits the different rest wavelengths. Both shifts are positive, so both sources recede. Therefore choose C.

steps.text: A $3.0\,\mathrm{eV}$ photon matches the $5.0-2.0\,\mathrm{eV}$ gap. The lower state of that transition must be populated. parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Use the release and first rebound to find the fraction of mechanical energy lost at the first impact.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Find the ratio of the speed immediately after this impact to the speed immediately before it.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Using the constant-retention model, predict the fifth rebound height from the release height.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: The measured fifth height is $(0.040\pm0.005)\,\mathrm m$. A propagated model prediction is $(0.086\pm0.007)\,\mathrm m$. Decide whether these data support the model, using the uncertainties.

parts.label: e
parts.prompt: A common calibration error makes every measured height $10\%$ too large. Explain its effect on the energy-retention fraction inferred from height ratios.

steps.text: Energy at a turning point is $mgh$. The retained fraction is $0.512/0.800=0.640$.
The fraction lost is $1-0.640=0.360$, or $36.0\%$.
Kinetic energy is proportional to speed squared; use $v_{\rm after}/v_{\rm before}=\sqrt{0.640}$.
The speed ratio is $0.800$.
The fifth rebound follows five impacts, so $h_5=0.800(0.640)^5$.
$h_5=0.0859\,\mathrm m$, approximately $0.086\,\mathrm m$.
The measured interval $[0.035,0.045]\,\mathrm m$ and predicted interval $[0.079,0.093]\,\mathrm m$ do not overlap.
The discrepancy is larger than the stated combined bounds, so the later result does not support constant retention over all five impacts. It does not identify a unique cause of failure.
Each ratio becomes $(1.10h_{n+1})/(1.10h_n)$.
The common factor cancels, so the inferred retention fraction is unchanged. Absolute heights and energy estimates would still be biased.

questions.answerSummary: (a) The fraction lost is $1-0.640=0.360$, or $36.0\%$.; (b) The speed ratio is $0.800$.; (c) $h_5=0.0859\,\mathrm m$, approximately $0.086\,\mathrm m$.; (d) The discrepancy is larger than the stated combined bounds, so the later result does not support constant retention over all five impacts. It does not identify a unique cause of failure.; (e) The common factor cancels, so the inferred retention fraction is unchanged. Absolute heights and energy estimates would still be biased.
